source_text: Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo ipse dicit: et omnis qui uidet et credit in me non morietur in aeternum? sed enim qui in hominem solitarium credit et nudum, maledictus dicitur: hic autem, qui credit in Christum non maledictus, sed in aeternum non moriturus refertur. ex quo sl ro aut homo est tantum, ut haeretici uolunt, quomodo quisquis in eum credit non morietur in aeternum, cum maledictus esse teneatur qui confidit in homine? aut si non maledictus, sed potius ad aeternae uitae consecutionem, ut legitur, destinatus, non homo tantummodo Christus, sed et deus; in quem qui credit, et maledictionis periculum deponit, et ad fructum iustitiae accedit. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo paracletum dicit de suo esse sumpturum quae nuntiaturus sit? neque enim paracletus ab homine quicquam accipit, sed homini scientiam paracletus porrigit; nec futura ab homine paracletus discit, sed de futuris hominem paracletus instruit. paraclitus a Christo homine quod nuntiet, quoniam paracleto homo nihil poterit dare a quo ipse homo debet accipere, et fallit in praesenti loco Christus et decipit, cum paracletum a se homine accepturum quae nuntiet dicit: aut non nos fallit, sicut nec fallit, et accepit paracletus a Christo quae nuntiet. sed si a Christo accepit quae nuntiet, maior ergo iam paracleto Christus est: quoniam nec paracletus a Christo acciperet, nisi minor Christo esset. minor autem Christo paracletus Christum etiam deum esse hoc ipso probat, a quo accepit quae nuntiat; ut testimonium Christo diuinitatis grande sit, dum minor Christo paraclitus repertus ab illo sumit quae ceteris tradit. quandoquidem si homo tantummodo Christus, a paracleto Christus acciperet quae diceret, non a Christo paracletus acciperet quae nuntiaret. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quare credendi nobis talem regulam posuit, quo diceret: haec est autem uita aeterna ut sciant te unum et uerum deum, et quem misisti Iesum Christum? si noluisset se etiam deum intellegi, cur addidit: e quem misisti Iesum Christum, nisi quoniam et deum accipi uoluit? quoniam si se deum nollet intellegi, addidisset: e quem misisti hominem Iesum Christum. nunc autem neque addidit, nec se hominem nobis tantummodo Christus tradidit, sed deo iunxit, ut et deum per hanc coniunctionem, sicut est, intellegi uellet. est ergo credendum, secundum praescriptam regulam, in dominum, unum uerum deum, et in eum quem misit Iesum Christum consequenter, qui se nequaquam patri, ut diximus, iunxisset, nisi deum quoque intellegi uellet. separasset enim ab eo, si deum intellegi se noluisset. inter homines enim tantummodo se collocasset, si hominem se esse tantummodo sciret, nec cum deo iunxisset, si se non et deum nosset. nunc et de homine tacet, quoniam hominem illum nemo dubitat, et deo se iungit merito, ut credituris diuinitatis suae formulam poneret. Si homo tantummodo Christus, quomodo dicit: e nunc honorifica me gloria quam habebam apud te priusquam mundus esset? si antequam mundus esset gloriam habuit apud deum et claritatem tenuit apud patrem, ante mundum fuit: nec enim habuisset gloriam, nisi ipse prius fuisset, qui gloriam posset tenere. nemo enim habere aliquid poterit, nisi ante ipse fuerit, qui aliquid tenet. sed enim Christus habet gloriam ante mundi institutionem; ergo ante institutionem mundi fuit. nisi enim ante institutionem mundi esset, ante mundi institutionem gloriam habere non posset, cum ipse non esset. sed enim homo gloriam ante mundi institutionem habere non potuit, qui post mundum fuit: Christus autem habuit: ante mundum igitur fuit. non igitur homo tantummodo fuit, qui ante mundum fuit: deus est igitur, quoniam ante mundum fuit et gloriam ante mundum tenuit. nec praedestinatio ista dicatur, quoniam nec posita est. aut addant hoc qui hoc putant. sed uae est adicientibus, quo modo et detrahentibus, positum. non potest ergo dici quod non potest adici. sublata ergo praedestinatione, quae non est posita, in substantia fuit Christus ante mundi institutionem. uerbum est enim per quod facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil, quoniam et si in praedestinatione dicitur gloriosus, et ante mundi institutionem fuisse praedestinationem, ordo seruetur, et ante hunc erit multus numerus hominum in gloriam minor enim per istam destinationem Christus ceteris intellegetur, quibus posterior denotatur. gloria in praedestinatione fuit, praedestinationem istam in gloriam nouissimus Christus accepit: ante enim praedestinatus Adam esse cernetur, et Abel, et Enoch, et Noe, et Abraham, et reliqui ceteri. nam cum apud deum et personarum et rerum omnium ordo digestus sit, ante hanc praedestinationem Christi in gloriam multi praedestinati fuisse dicentur, et hoc pacto minor ceteris hominibus Christus esse deprehendetur, qui melior et maior et antiquior ipsis quoque angelis inuenitur. aut haec igitur omnia tollantur, ut Christo diuinitas auferatur: aut si haec tolli non possunt, Christo ab haereticis diuinitas propria reddatur.
pass_a_gloss: If Christ is only a man, how does He say that everyone who sees and believes in Him will not die eternally? But indeed, the one who believes in a solitary and naked man is said to be cursed. However, the one who believes in Christ is not cursed, but rather is said to be one who will not die eternally. From this, if Christ is only a man, as the heretics want, how can it be that whoever believes in Him will not die eternally, when the one who trusts in a man is held to be cursed? Or if the one who believes in Christ is not cursed, but rather is destined for the attainment of eternal life, as it is written, then Christ is not only a man, but also God. The one who believes in Him both puts aside the danger of curse and attains the fruit of righteousness. If Christ is only a man, how can He say that He will take from His own what the Paraclete will announce? For the Paraclete does not receive anything from a man, but rather the Paraclete imparts knowledge to men. The Paraclete does not learn future things from a man, but rather instructs men about future things. If the Paraclete receives from Christ, who is a man, what He will announce, then Christ is greater than the Paraclete. For the Paraclete would not receive from Christ unless He were lesser than Christ. The fact that the Paraclete is lesser than Christ and receives from Him what He announces proves that Christ is also God. This is a great testimony to Christ's divinity, since the Paraclete, who is lesser than Christ, receives from Him what He imparts to others. If Christ is only a man, why did He give us such a rule of faith, saying: 'This is eternal life, that they may know You, the one and true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent'? If He did not want to be understood as God, why did He add 'whom You have sent, Jesus Christ'? For if He did not want to be understood as God, He would have added 'whom You have sent, the man Jesus Christ'. But He did not add this, and Christ did not present Himself to us as only a man, but rather joined Himself to God, so that He might be understood as God through this conjunction. Therefore, according to the prescribed rule, we must believe in the Lord, the one and true God, and in Jesus Christ, whom He sent. If Christ is only a man, how can He say: 'Now glorify me with the glory that I had with You before the world existed'? For if He had glory with God before the world existed, He existed before the world. No one can have something unless they existed before. But Christ had glory before the institution of the world, therefore He existed before the institution of the world. Unless He existed before the institution of the world, He could not have had glory before the institution of the world, since He Himself did not exist. But a man could not have had glory before the institution of the world, since he came after the world. Christ, however, had glory, therefore He existed before the world. He is not only a man, who existed before the world, but also God, since He existed before the world and had glory before the world. This is not a predestination, since it is not something that has been established. Those who think this should add it, but woe to those who add or subtract. What cannot be added cannot be said. Therefore, with the predestination, which is not established, being set aside, Christ existed in substance before the institution of the world. For He is the Word through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Even if it is said that He is glorious in predestination, and that predestination existed before the institution of the world, the order is preserved, and before this, there will be a great number of men in glory, for Christ will be understood to be lesser than those to whom He is posterior. The glory was in predestination, and Christ, who is the last, received this predestination in glory. For before this predestination of Christ in glory, many were predestined, such as Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and the rest. For since the order of persons and things is established with God, before this predestination of Christ in glory, many will be said to have been predestined, and in this way, Christ will be found to be lesser than other men, who are better, greater, and more ancient than the angels themselves. Either all these things must be abolished, so that Christ's divinity may be taken away, or if these things cannot be abolished, then Christ's divinity must be restored to Him by the heretics.

pass_b_english: If Christ is only a man, how can he say: 'And everyone who sees and believes in me will not die eternally'? Yet the one who believes in a solitary and naked man is pronounced cursed; but the one who believes in Christ is not cursed, but is said to be one who will not die forever. From this it follows: if Christ is only a man, as the heretics want, how can whoever believes in him avoid eternal death, when the one who trusts in a man is held to be cursed? Or if the believer in Christ is not cursed but rather destined for the attainment of eternal life, as it is written, then Christ is not only a man but also God; for the one who believes in him both sets aside the danger of curse and advances to the fruit of righteousness. If Christ is only a man, how can he say that the Paraclete will take from his own what he will announce? For the Paraclete does not receive anything from a man, but imparts knowledge to men; the Paraclete does not learn future things from a man, but instructs men about future things. If the Paraclete were to receive from Christ-as-man what he is to announce, then Christ would be deceiving and misleading us in this very passage, since a man could give nothing to the Paraclete from whom the man himself must receive. But Christ does not deceive us, any more than he deceives, and the Paraclete has received from Christ what he will announce. Since the Paraclete has received from Christ what he announces, Christ is therefore greater than the Paraclete; for the Paraclete would not receive from Christ unless he were lesser than Christ. The fact that the Paraclete is lesser than Christ and receives from him what he proclaims proves that Christ is also God. This is a great testimony to Christ's divinity, since the Paraclete, found to be lesser than Christ, takes from him what he hands on to others. If Christ were only a man, then Christ would receive from the Paraclete what he would say, not the Paraclete from Christ.

If Christ is only a man, why did he lay down for us such a rule of belief, saying: 'This is eternal life, that they may know you, the one and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent' (John 17:3)? If he had not wished to be understood as God also, why did he add 'whom you have sent, Jesus Christ'? For if he had not wished to be understood as God, he would have added 'whom you have sent, the man Jesus Christ.' But he did not add this, and Christ did not present himself to us as only a man, but joined himself to God, so that through this conjunction he might be understood as God, as he is. Therefore it must be believed, according to the prescribed rule, in the Lord, the one true God, and in the one whom he sent, Jesus Christ, consequently; for he would not have joined himself to the Father, as we said, unless he also wished to be understood as God. He would have separated himself from the Father if he had not wished himself to be understood as God. For he would have placed himself among men only, if he knew himself to be only a man, and he would not have joined himself to God if he did not also know himself to be God. Now he is silent about the man, because no one doubts that he is a man, and he joins himself to God deservedly, so that he might set a formula of his divinity for believers.

If Christ is only a man, how can he say: 'Now glorify me, Father, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed' (John 17:5)? If he had glory with God before the world existed and held splendor with the Father, then he existed before the world; for no one can have something unless he himself existed before, he who holds it. But Christ has glory before the institution of the world; therefore he existed before the institution of the world. For unless he existed before the institution of the world, he could not have had glory before the institution of the world, since he himself did not exist. Yet a man could not have had glory before the institution of the world, who came after the world; but Christ had it: therefore he was before the world. He is therefore not only a man, who was before the world; he is God, since he was before the world and held glory before the world. Let this not be called predestination, since it is not established. Let those who think this add it. But woe to those who add, just as to those who subtract, what is established. It cannot be said that what cannot be added is possible. Therefore, with predestination, which is not established, set aside, Christ existed in substance before the institution of the world. For he is the Word through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. And even if it is said that he is glorious in predestination, and that predestination existed before the institution of the world, the order is preserved, and before this there will be a great number of men in glory; for Christ will be understood to be lesser through this destination than the rest, to whom he is posterior. Glory was in predestination, and Christ, who is the last, received this predestination in glory; for before this predestination of Christ in glory, Adam is seen to have been predestined, and Abel, and Enoch, and Noah, and Abraham, and the rest. For since with God the order of all persons and things is settled, before this predestination of Christ in glory many will be said to have been predestined, and in this way Christ will be found to be lesser than other men, who are better, greater, and more ancient than the angels themselves. Either all these things must be abolished, so that Christ's divinity may be taken away, or if these things cannot be abolished, Christ's own divinity must be restored to him by the heretics.
